newsitem.title: BELGIUM: NATO tries to make left-out east Europeans feel in.
newsitem.headline: NATO tries to make left-out east Europeans feel in.

text.p: NATO tried on Friday to reassure disappointed eastern European countries they were part of the new security order despite being excluded from the alliance's first expansion behind the old Iron Curtain.

As Slovenia and Romania took in the news that the United States had decided they should stay out for the time being, NATO defence ministers told the counterparts from 27 "partnership" nations their presence and involvement at NATO headquarters would be increasingly important.

Taking the United States' NATO allies by surprise, U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen announced on Thursday only Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary should be invited to membership talks at the NATO Madrid Summit set for July 8-9. Twelve have applied.

Faced with a smaller expansion into the former communist bloc than many would have liked, NATO defence ministers placed the emphasis on Friday on a growing role for the Partnership for Peace programme, which links 27 countries from Azerbaijan to Albania to NATO's peacekeeping acitivities.
"The family keeps on getting bigger," one NATO source said, as neutral Switzerland turned up at NATO headquarters for the first time in the form of Defence Minister Adolf Ogi.

At a first meeting of the Partnership Council the 27 were told they would be expected to set up missions in Brussels and send ambassadors and would be involved from the beginning in peace planning operations.

NATO Secretary General Javier Solana forecast the NATO workforce would double over the next two years to 6,000 from 3,000, putting a strain of the headquarters, which straggle along a suburban Brussels main road.
The reassurances seemed too little for a rejected Slovenia, whose defence minister Turnsek Tit said all countries meeting membership criteria should be been invited in.
"If the door is to be open it would be good if it was to open again soon," a NATO official quoted him as saying in reaction to assurances that the first NATO enlargement would not be the last.

Although Washington's decision is expected to be decisive, some European partners have vowed to continue pushing the Slovenian and Romanian bids. The two countries have also vowed to try to make President Bill Clinton change his mind.
France and the supporters of a broader expansion argue that the two countries need to be included in order to maintain a balance between NATO's northern and southern flanks.

The NATO and eastern defence ministers also discussed Bosnia and agreed they should do all they could to move towards civilian implementation of the Dayton Peace Accord, but stressed the NATO stabilisation force SFOR could not become a reconstruction agency.
